Stated Claim / Post Context:
Facing political headwinds, Oregon Republicans lean into ‘ballot harvesting’

=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: Facing political headwinds, Oregon Republicans lean into ‘ballot harvesting’ ===

[Source 1 — www.opb.org] (URL: https://www.opb.org/article/2026/10/30/oregon-politics-ballot-voting-election-republicans-democrats/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Facing political headwinds, Oregon Republicans lean into ‘ballot harvesting’

Members of the party have recently criticized the practice of turning in ballots on behalf of sympathetic voters.

Actual Article Body:
Independent. Member-supported.For the Pacific Northwest.

Independent.Member-supported.

Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Stay informed with OPB on the Oregon governor's race and other regional contests in Oregon and Southwest Washington at our ballot guide.

An election worker opens a ballot at the Clackamas County Elections Office in Oregon City, Ore., Nov. 5, 2024. Election workers are responsible for verifying signatures, removing ballots from their envelopes, examining ballots for potential problems, and tallying the number of ballots received. The ballots are then scanned by a machine that records votes.

Anna Lueck for OPB

This Halloween, Oregon Republicans will be going door to door looking like Democrats — at least in action.

In legislative battlegrounds around the state, a small army of GOP volunteers are planning to fan out, knock doors, and offer to turn voters’ ballots in for them.

It’s a perfectly legal practice in Oregon, so long as you follow basic rules. But “ballot harvesting,” as it’s sometimes known, has more often been the province of Democrats and their allies. Republicans have previously looked askance at corralling ballots, even pressing to make it illegal.

Not this year. With the GOP staring down the possibility of losing more ground in the Legislature and a high-stakes governor’s race on the line, some say it’s time to pull out the stops to juice Republican turnout.

“It’s really just about getting out the vote,” said Senate Minority Leader Bruce Starr, R-Dundee, who supports the effort. “Republicans will win this election if every Republican ballot is turned in and every common-sense nonaffiliated voter votes.”

The effort is being spearheaded via a new committee, GOTV OREGON PAC, formed by a group of Republican political operatives and boosters. On a website announcing its intentions, the group says it aims to find 1,000 volunteers to chase ballots in competitive legislative districts — including areas of Clackamas County, the North Coast, the Columbia River Gorge, and Marion County.

Organizers say they’ll be primarily urging likely Republican voters to get their ballots in. But they’ll also be offering to turn in ballots for voters who are willing to hand them over.

“Maybe some people don’t give up their ballot, but it doesn’t mean that we’re not handing them material that says, ‘Here’s where the drop boxes are. Here’s who we think you should vote for,’” said Bryan Iverson, a Republican political consultant and legislative staffer who is helping to coordinate the new strategy.

It’s a common critique of Oregon Republicans that they are routinely outmaneuvered by a Democratic ground game that turns out hundreds of volunteers — many from labor unions or other allied groups — to knock doors and urge sympathetic voters to turn in their ballot.

Iverson says he relearned the lesson in 2024, when a Republican Senate candidate he was working for, Raymond Love, recruited dozens of people to knock doors in an attempt to unseat state Sen. Chris Gorsek, D-Gresham.

“And then the next weekend I see a photo with Chris Gorsek and 300 people all wearing SEIU T-shirts,” Iverson said, referring to the state’s largest labor group, Service Employees International Union. “We can’t beat them if they’re out there just scooping up ballots at the last minute.”

In fact, Democratic campaigns are not ballot harvesting this year, and haven’t for several election cycles, said Tom Crawford, a spokesman for the Democratic Party of Oregon. Democrats do run a robust get-out-the-vote operation with allied groups in the days leading up to the election.

“Democratic Party of Oregon volunteers and staff are focused on helping voters get their ballots filed out and turned in by Election Day,” Crawford said.

Turning in ballots on behalf of voters can bring perils if not done with care, one possible reason why it appears to have gone out of fashion with Democrats.

In 2018, a labor-affiliated group revealed it had misplaced a stack of nearly 100 ballots from the November election, failing to get them in a drop box in in time to be counted. That ran afoul of a state law that requires anyone turning in a ballot on behalf of another person to do so within two days.

The group that made the error, Defend Oregon, ultimately avoided much of a nearly $95,000 state fine issued because of the gaffe.

Democrats OPB spoke with said the party hasn’t done much ballot harvesting since, saying it brings high risk for relatively little reward. But Republicans have made the practice a talking point anyway.

Two candidates for governor in this year’s Republican primary signaled they wanted to outlaw it.

And the eventual winner of that contest, state Sen. Christine Drazan, introduced a bill to ban ballot harvesting while serving in the House last year. It went nowhere in the Democratically controlled House, and The Portland Mercury reported in August that Drazan’s campaign for governor has discussed using the tactic to boost turnout this year.

A spokeswoman for Drazan’s campaign did not respond to an inquiry Friday. Starr described the GOTV Oregon effort as “complimentary” to Drazan’s campaign, not directly connected.

Whatever their history on the issue, legislative Republicans appear all in on a strategy that includes ballot collection this year. Six GOP lawmakers have kicked in campaign funds to GOTV OREGON PAC, which has reported raising roughly $60,000.

Iverson said the campaign will pay people who want to work extended shifts in the runup to Election Day — it’s offering up to $35 an hour. But he said the effort is largely relying on volunteers, who have signed up for more than 1,000 two-hour shifts.

Whether or not the effort pays off will be answered after Election Day. But in a year when Democrats appear to have momentum, Iverson says even an extraordinary get-out-the-vote operation might not be enough.

“If I was a Democrat, I’d be cautiously optimistic,” he said. “I don’t think I’d be bullish, but they’re not going backwards. That’s probably a fair statement.”

An Oregon elementary school teacher who fought a teenage gunman during a deadly school shooting earlier this month has broken her silence, describing the tragedy as a loss she will carry with her forever.

Cassidy Schutz, a certified learning specialist at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, released her first public statement Friday through Bend-La Pine Schools, just over two weeks after the Oct. 15 attack left three children and a teacher dead.

"There are no words to describe the depth of sadness I am feeling following the events of October 15th. This is not a story. This is a horrific and heartbreaking tragedy, and it is our real lives," Schutz said in the statement.

HERO DAD WHO TOOK DOWN OREGON SCHOOL SHOOTER IDENTIFIED ALONG WITH TEACHER, STUDENT BOTH KILLED IN ATTACK

Cassidy Schutz, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., fought a gunman during the Oct. 15 school shooting that killed three students and a teacher. (Bend-La Pine Schools)

"My thoughts are with those who were lost, their families, those who were hurt, and those who were there that day. My heart is with you. It all happened so fast, and I wish with everything in me that we had more time. The pain of this loss I will carry with me forever."

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz previously credited Schutz with throwing her cellphone at the shooter and wrestling him for control of his shotgun during the attack.

Schutz also asked for privacy as she continues to heal.

INJURED BEND, OREGON, TEACHER TRIED TO SHUT CLASSROOM DOOR DURING SCHOOL SHOOTING BEFORE PLAYING DEAD

Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., Oct. 16, a day after a deadly shooting. (Haven Daley/AP Photo)

"There are no words for this unimaginable reality we are facing. My focus is on these families, our team, our school, and my own healing," she said. "As I continue to navigate this, I ask that you please give me the time, space, and privacy I need to heal. I will not be making any additional public statements at this time."

The shooting unfolded when a 16-year-old former student entered the school and opened fire inside a classroom serving students with special needs, according to police.

Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, and three students, including 5-year-old Rhoam Summer and two other children, ages 8 and 11, were killed.

DEMOCRATS' LATEST GUN-CONTROL PUSH RUNS INTO INCONVENIENT FACT ABOUT HOW SCHOOL KILLER WAS STOPPED

Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place Oct. 15, in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)

Another teacher, Becky Drury, and a 7-year-old girl were wounded but survived.

Drury previously told Fox News Digital she tried to close her classroom door after spotting the gunman but was shot before she could stop him from entering.

She suffered severe injuries to both arms and pretended to be dead to avoid being shot again before hero dad Kaylub Giamanco, 36, shot the attacker dead.
